Heard the submission of Sri T. Pradyumna Kumar Reddy, learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of Mr. Apurva M. Gokhale, learned counsel on record for the petitioner as well as the learned Public Prosecutor, who is appearing for respondents 1 and 2.
Gave anxious consideration to their submissions as well as the contents of the decisions that are relied upon by the learned counsel for the petitioner.

2. Seeking to quash the proceedings that are initiated against the petitioner, who is arrayed as accused No.3 in C.C.No.784 of 2012 that is pending on the file of the Court of I Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Nampally, Hyderabad, the petitioner filed the present application.

sentences.text:
Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the complaint itself is not maintainable as per the contents of the Insecticides Act, 1968 and therefore, continuation of proceedings against the petitioner, who is accused No.3 in 4 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 the said Calendar Case, is unwarranted and therefore, the same has to be quashed.

2 3.

On the other hand, learned Public Prosecutor submits that on analysis, the sample drawn was found to be misbranded and therefore, a complaint was lodged by the Agricultural Officer,
Hyderabad, against the petitioner and others and therefore, the present petition is unsustainable.

4. In the light of the aforementioned submissions, the point that evolves for consideration is:
Whether there exists any justifiable ground to invoke the power granted under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and to quash the proceedings that are pending against the petitioner/A.3 in C.C.No.784 of 2012 on the file of the Court of I Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Nampally, Hyderabad?

sentences.text:
5. The case of the complainant, as could be seen from the complaint, is that on 14.03.2011, the Agricultural Officer (Technical), Hyderabad, visited the premises of M/s. Vanasri Seeds Pvt. Ltd.,
which is located in D.No.3-6- 308/1, Hyderguda, Hyderabad and has drawn six insecticide samples.
The samples drawn were duly sealed 5 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 and packed, as provided under law and a report was also prepared.
The said samples were sent to Insecticide Analyst for analysis.
The Insecticide Analyst declared Fenazaquin 10% EC as misbranded.
By the time the Analyst report was received, the sample got expired.
Therefore, there was no chance for reanalysis of the sample.
Thus, the accused including the petitioner, who is arrayed as accused No.3, have committed the offences punishable under Section 29(1)(a) of the Insecticides Act, 1968.

6. The one and only point urged by the learned Senior Counsel is that by the contents of the complaint itself it is clear that there was no chance for reanalysis of the sample as by the time Analyst submitted his report, the sample got expired and thus, the right of the petitioner/A.3 for getting the sample reanalyzed was lost and therefore, on the principle of violation of statutory right,
further proceedings are unsustainable.
Learned counsel brought to the notice of this Court the contents of Section 24 of the Insecticides Act.

As per the said provision, there is every necessity on the part of the Insecticide Analyst to submit his report to 6 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 the Insecticide Inspector within a period of thirty days from the date the sample was submitted to him for analysis.
It is also laid down that the Insecticide Inspector has to deliver one copy of the report to the person from whom the sample was taken.
It is further narrated that the said person, within a period of 28 days from the date of receipt of copy of the report, can exhibit his intention to adduce evidence in contravention of the report.

Section 24(4) of the Insecticides Act, 1968, further states that when such person exhibits his intention to adduce evidence in contravention of the Insecticide Analyst report, the Court may on its own motion or in its discretion at the request either of the complainant or of the accused, cause the sample of the insecticide sent for test or analysis to the Central Insecticide Laboratory.

For the convenience of discussion and fruitful analysis, Section 24 of the Insecticides Act, 1968 is extracted as under:
Report of Insecticide Analyst:-
(1) The Insecticide Analyst to whom a sample of any insecticide has been submitted for test or analysis under sub-section (6) of Section 22, shall, within a period of thirty days, deliver to the Insecticide Inspector Mr. Ram Krishna Mudholkar, vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh, on 21 February, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107593384/
3 7 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 submitting it a signed report in duplicate in the prescribed form.
(2) The Insecticide Inspector on receipt thereof shall deliver one copy of the report to the person form whom the sample was taken and shall retain the other copy for use in any prosecution in respect of the sample.

(3) Any document purporting to be a report signed by an Insecticide Analyst shall be evidence of the facts stated therein, and such evidence shall be conclusive unless the person from whom the sample was taken has within twenty-eight days of the receipt of a copy of the report notified in writing the Insecticide Inspector or the court before which any proceedings in respect of the sample are pending that he intends to adduce evidence in controversion of the report.

(4) Unless the sample has already been tested or analyzed in the Central Laboratory, where a person has under sub-section (3) notified his intention of adducing evidence in controversion of the Insecticide Analyst's report, the Court may, of its own motion or in its discretion at the request either of the complainant or of the accused, cause the sample of the insecticide produced before the Magistrate under sub-section (6) of section 22 to be sent for test or analysis to the said laboratory,
(which shall, within a period of thirty days, which shall make the test or analysis) and report in writing signed by, or under the authority of, the Director of the Central Insecticides Laboratory the result thereof, and such report shall be conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein."
8

Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 (5) The cost of a test or analysis made by the Central Insecticides Laboratory under sub- section (4) shall be paid by the complainant or the accused, as the court shall direct."
7.

A crucial point which requires a mention here is that by Act 23 of 2000 which came into effect from 05.08.2000, by which certain amendments were made to Insecticides Act, 1968, the time to submit report by Insecticide Analyst to Insecticide Inspector has been reduced from sixty days to thirty days.

8. Though Section 24 of the Insecticides Act, 1968, appears to be identical to Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, which is to be read with Rule 7 of Food Adulteration Rules, yet there is no provision in Food Adulteration Act of serving of copy of Analyst report to the person from whom the sample is drawn before the complaint is lodged.
However, under Section 24 of the Insecticides Act, 1968, such a facility is provided.

Section 24(2) of the Insecticides Act, 1968,
clearly lays down that the Insecticide Inspector on receipt of the report from the Insecticide Analyst deliver one copy of the report to the 9 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 person from whom the sample was taken.
However, in the case on hand, the Agricultural Officer, who presented the complaint made a clear mention that by the time Analyst report was received, the sample got expired.

9. Catena of decisions of the Hon'ble Apex Court and this Court emphasizes that there is every requirement that the samples drawn be tested either by the State Analyst notified for that purpose or by the Central Analyst within its shelf life.
The words 'shelf life' and 'best before date' are well explained under the provisions of the Food Adulteration Act.

Submitting that in similar situations,

sentences.text: the Hon'ble Apex Court held that the proceedings are unsustainable as the valuable right of the accused for getting the sample reanalyzed is lost due to the acts of the complainant, learned counsel for the petitioner relied upon three decisions.

The first decision is the one that is rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Gupta Chemicals Private Limited and Others v. State of 10 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 Rajasthan and another1 wherein the Court at paragraph Nos.11 to 13 of the judgment held as follows:-
"From our perusal of the afore quoted provisions it is manifest that ordinarily in the absence of any material to the contrary, the report of the insecticides analyst will be accepted as final and conclusive of the material contained therewith.

entities.text: Gupta Chemicals Private Limited and Others v. State of 10 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 Rajasthan and another1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This is however subject to the right of the accused to have the sample examined by the central insecticides laboratory provided he communicates his intentions for the purpose within 28 days of the receipt of the copy of the report.

It needs no emphasis that this right vested under the statutes valuable for the defence, particularly in a case where the allegations are that the material does not conform to the prescribed standard.

As noted earlier in the present case the appellants had intimated the insecticide inspector their intention to have the sample tested in the central insecticides laboratory within the prescribed period of 28 days of receipt of the copy of the state analyst report, yet no step was taken by the inspector either to send the sample to the central insecticides laboratory or to file the complaint in the court with promptitude in which case the appellants would have moved the magistrate for appropriate order for the purpose.

The resultant position is that due to sheer inaction on the part of the inspector, it has not been possible for the appellants to have the sample examined by the central insecticides laboratory and in the meantime, the shelf-life of the sample of insecticide seized had expired and for that reason no further step could be taken for its examination.
In the circumstances, we are of the view that continuing this criminal prosecution against the appellant will be a futile exercise and abuse of the process of court.
The High Court was not right in 1 (2010) 7 SCC 735 11 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 dismissing the petition filed under Section 482 of Cr.P.C.
Accordingly
, the appeals are allowed, the orders passed by the High Court are set aside and the prosecution alleged against the appellants are quashed."

The second one is the decision rendered by the same Court in the case between Northern Mineral Limited v. Union of india and another2, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court at paragraph No.25 held as follows:
"It may be mentioned herein that shelf life of the insecticides had expired even prior to the filing of the complaint.

sentences.text:
The position therefore which emerges is that by sheer inaction the shelf life of the sample of insecticides had expired and for that reason no step was possible to be taken for its test and analysis by Central Insecticides Mr. Ram Krishna Mudholkar, vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh, on 21 February, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107593384/
5

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Laboratory.

Valuable right of the appellant having been defeated, we are of the opinion that allowing this criminal prosecution against the appellant to continue shall be futile and abuse of the process of Court."

The third decision is also from the Hon'ble Apex Court in a case between State of Haryana v. Unique Farmaid Ltd. and Others3, wherein the Court at paragraph No.12 held as follows:
"It cannot be gainsaid, therefore, that the respondents in these appeals have been deprived of their valuable right to have the sample tested from the Central Insecticides Laboratory under Sub- 2 (2010) 7 SCC 726 3 (1999) 8 SCC 190 12 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 section (4) of Section 24 of the Act.

entities.text: State of Haryana v. Unique Farmaid Ltd.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Under Sub- section (3) of Section 24 report signed by the Insecticide analyst shall be evidence of the facts stated therein and shall be conclusive evidence against the accused only if the accused do not, within 28 days of the receipt of the report, notify in writing to the Insecticides Inspector or the Court before which proceedings are pending that they intend to adduce evidence to controvert the report.
In the present cases Insecticide Inspector was notified that the accused intended to adduce evidence to controvert the report.
By the time the matter reached the court, shelf life of the sample had already expired and no purpose would have been served informing the court of such an intention.
The report of the Insecticide Analyst was, therefore, not conclusive.

A valuable right had been conferred on the accused to have the sample tested from the central Insecticides Laboratory and in the circumstances of the case accused have been deprived of that right, thus, prejudicing them in their defence.
In these circumstances, High Court was right in concluding that it will be an abuse of the process of court if the prosecution is continued against the respondent - the accused person.
High Court rightly quashed the criminal complaint.

We uphold the order of the High Court and would dismiss the appeals."
10. Section 24 of the Insecticides Act makes a clear mention that the report of the Insecticide Analyst is a conclusive proof unless and until it is challenged and when it is challenged and the report of the Central Insecticides Laboratory is produced, the report of the said Laboratory would be a conclusive proof.
Thus, it is clear that the 13 Dr.CSL,J CRL.P.NO.2936 OF 2013 report of the Central Insecticides Laboratory supersedes the report of the Insecticide Analyst.
The same is the position as envisaged under Section 13(4) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

Thus, it can undoubtedly be held that getting sample reanalyzed by Central Insecticides Laboratory is a valuable statutory right which is conferred upon the persons against whom accusations are proposed to be made before the Court of law.
When such a right is denied, it can unhesitatingly be held that such proceedings are unsustainable and cannot be permitted to be continued putting the accused to sufferance.

The ultimate conclusion that would be drawn even after conducting trial would be that the accused are liable to be acquitted basing on the technical error and the mistake committed by the prosecuting agency.
Therefore, this Court is of the view that there exist justifiable grounds for quashing the proceedings as sought for by the petitioner.
